h1: Worty taste in finished beer and what it says about fermentation
title: Worty Taste in Finished Beer Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: Why a finished beer can taste of sweet, raw wort, what it says about fermentation and the tests brewers use to find the cause.
teaser: A worty finished beer tastes like the sample you pulled from the kettle. That is the fermentation telling you it did not finish its job.
standfirst: Worty flavour is the taste of wort that never fully became beer: sweet, grainy, a little like porridge or malt extract. It is common in young, rushed or stalled beers and in many non-alcoholic beers. Here is what it means and how to diagnose it.
sections:
Anyone who has tasted wort straight from the kettle knows the flavour: sweet, cereal, slightly like malted milk powder, porridge or a malt extract drink. In finished beer that character should be gone, replaced by the cleaner malt flavour of fermented beer. When it lingers, tasters call the beer worty.

Worty is partly about sugar and partly about aroma. Residual sugar gives sweetness and body. The aroma comes largely from aldehydes, including 2-methylbutanal, 3-methylbutanal and methional, which carry malty, cooked potato and wort-like notes. Yeast reduces those aldehydes during a healthy fermentation. When the yeast does not get the chance, they stay.

Worty beer almost always means a fermentation that was weak, short or stopped early. The common causes:

  • Underpitching. Too few healthy cells for the wort gravity. A lager needs roughly twice the pitch rate of an ale of the same gravity.
  • Low oxygen at pitching. Without oxygen to build membranes, yeast runs out of steam.
  • Crashing too early. Cooling the tank before fermentation is truly finished, often to free up a vessel.
  • Poor yeast health. Old slurry, low viability or a strain stressed by high gravity.
  • Temperature drops. A fermentation that cools sharply, or a glycol fault overnight, can send the yeast to the bottom before it finishes.

All of these leave both residual sugar and unreduced aldehydes, which is why worty beer often tastes sweet and grainy at once. Our guide to grainy and husky notes in pale lager covers the overlap.
Read the gravity log before you taste

A worty beer has usually left clues in the fermentation log long before anyone tastes it. A healthy ale at 18 to 20 °C typically drops most of its gravity in the first three or four days, then slows. A lager at 10 to 12 °C takes longer, but the curve has the same shape. Warning signs are a lag of more than a day before gravity moves, a curve that flattens early or two readings a day apart that do not change while the gravity is still well above target.

Breweries that log gravity daily, or use an inline density sensor, can spot a stalling tank and act while the yeast is still in suspension: rousing it, raising the temperature a couple of degrees or holding off the crash. A brewery that takes one reading at the end only finds out at packaging.

The cleanest way to tell a stalled fermentation from a wort that simply had less fermentable sugar is the forced fermentation test, also called the limit attenuation test. Take a sample of the wort at knockout, pitch it heavily with yeast, keep it warm at about 25 °C and shake or stir it. Within a day or two it ferments as far as it possibly can. Its final gravity is the limit.

Compare that limit with the main tank:

  • If the tank finished at or close to the limit, the fermentation did its job and the sweetness comes from the wort itself, through mash temperature or recipe.
  • If the tank finished several points above the limit, the yeast stopped early. Look at pitch rate, oxygen, temperature and yeast health.

This one test ends a lot of arguments between the brewhouse and the cellar.
Worty is not the same as diacetyl or acetaldehyde

Young beer can carry several green flavours at once. Worty is sweet and cereal. Diacetyl is butter or butterscotch with a slick mouthfeel, covered in our guide to diacetyl. Acetaldehyde is green apple or freshly cut pumpkin. All three point to fermentation that needed more time or more vigour and they often appear together in a rushed beer. Telling them apart tells you which part of yeast metabolism fell short.
Why non-alcoholic beers often taste worty

Many non-alcoholic beers made by limited fermentation, where yeast is stopped early or a strain that ferments little sugar is used, have a worty character for exactly the reason above. The yeast never got far enough to reduce the wort aldehydes. Producers work on mash design, special yeast strains and careful hopping to cover it. Beers made by removing alcohol from a fully fermented beer tend to taste less worty, though dealcoholisation brings its own challenges.
What to change on the next batch

Once you know the fermentation stopped short, the fixes are standard:

  • Count cells and check viability before pitching, rather than pitching by volume.
  • Oxygenate to the usual 8 to 10 mg/L for ales and check with a meter.
  • Do not crash until gravity has held steady for two or three days and a diacetyl check passes.
  • Keep fermentation temperature steady, which in an Indian summer means glycol capacity sized for the hottest month, not the average one.

Your first step: run a forced fermentation test on your next brew alongside the main tank and write both final gravities on the brew sheet. That comparison will tell you whether worty beer is a recipe problem or a yeast problem.
faqs: What does worty mean in beer?
It means the beer tastes of unfermented wort: sweet, grainy and like malt extract. It usually points to incomplete fermentation.
Underpitching, low oxygen, poor yeast health, temperature drops or crashing the tank too early. Residual sugar and unreduced aldehydes are left behind.
How do brewers test for a stalled fermentation?
With a forced fermentation test: pitch a wort sample heavily, keep it warm and compare its final gravity with the main tank.
Why do some non-alcoholic beers taste worty?
Limited fermentation leaves wort aldehydes the yeast never reduced. Dealcoholised beers tend to show less of it.
